title: Regex: Extract Error Codes From a Log
oneLiner: Find every error code of the form ERR- plus exactly four digits in a log, as a whole token, using a regular expression in C# or Python.
keyTakeaway: Describe the shape, not the search: \bERR-[0-9]{4}\b finds the codes in one call (Regex.Matches / re.findall). The word boundaries \b stop matches glued to other letters or digits, and {4} with the closing \b rejects five-digit codes. Write [0-9] rather than \d when you mean ASCII digits.
explanation:
Write ExtractErrorCodes(log), which returns every error code in a block of log text, in the order they appear, duplicates included. An error code is the capital letters ERR, a hyphen, and exactly four digits, standing as a whole token: the character before it (if any) and the character after it (if any) must not be a letter, digit or underscore. So "(ERR-1042)" and "ERR-1042." count, but "XERR-1042", "ERR-10420" and "ERR-1042a" don't, and neither does lower-case "err-1042".

This is the job regular expressions are for: describe what the text looks like and let the engine find it. The pattern is \bERR-[0-9]{4}\b. \b is a word boundary, the point between a word character (letter, digit, underscore) and anything else, or the start or end of the text. ERR- is literal. [0-9]{4} is exactly four digits. In C#, Regex.Matches(log, pattern) returns every match and m.Value is the matched text; in Python, re.findall(pattern, log) returns the matched strings directly when the pattern has no groups.

Write the pattern as a verbatim string in C# (@"...") and a raw string in Python (r"..."), so the backslashes reach the regex engine instead of being read as string escapes: in a normal string "\b" is a backspace character. Prefer [0-9] to \d here: in both .NET and Python 3, \d also matches digits from other scripts, such as Arabic-Indic numerals.

The visualization runs the pattern over a short log and shows each match as it is found, and the near misses the boundaries reject.

visualizationSteps.message: The log, split into words only for display. The pattern \bERR-[0-9]{4}\b scans the raw text, not the words.
Match at index 0: ERR-1042. A boundary before ERR (start of text or a non-word character) and after the four digits.
XERR-2000 is skipped: X and E are both word characters, so there is no \b before ERR.
ERR-30001 is skipped: after four digits comes a fifth, so the closing \b fails.
Match at index 43: ERR-4004. A boundary before ERR (start of text or a non-word character) and after the four digits.
Done: two codes. The bracket in (ERR-4004) is not a word character, so the boundaries hold.

recognitionSignals: Pull every token of a fixed shape (IDs, codes, dates, IP addresses) out of free text.
Validate that a whole string has a format, using ^...$ or Regex.IsMatch / re.fullmatch.
gotchas: Without \b, ERR-[0-9]{4} also finds ERR-1234 inside ERR-12345 and XERR-1234.
A regex in a normal (non-raw) string loses its backslashes, or turns \b into a backspace.
Python's re.findall returns the groups, not the whole match, when the pattern contains (...); use (?:...) or no groups.
confusableWith: Regular Expression Matching (dp-regex-matching) asks you to build a tiny regex engine for . and * with dynamic programming; here you use the language's engine.
Splitting on spaces and checking each token misses codes next to punctuation, such as (ERR-1042) or ERR-1042.

complexity.note: The regex engine scans the n characters of the log once for this pattern (no nested quantifiers, so no backtracking blow-up); the list of matches holds at most O(n) characters.
